newsitem.title: USA: In Chase/Chemical bank merger, marketing challenges.
newsitem.headline: In Chase/Chemical bank merger, marketing challenges.

text.p: By Isadore Barmash
Chemical Bank this month became Chase, capping the largest bank merger in American history and creating big-time challenges for the merged company's marketers.
The peculiar twist of the $10-billion merger was that the larger company, with 612 branches, took the name of the smaller one.
In addition, customers had to be convinced that the megamerger of assets totalling almost $300 billion would benefit them, not just the banks' executives and shareholders.
"Our whole effort was aimed at telling our customers not to worry -- that it is our merger, not their's," said Lee Wilson, managing director of all of Chase's consumer marketing.
"In various advertisements, letters, brochures and other communications, we said that we would be more personal, more flexible, more responsive to their needs."

This was backed up by supplying "good news" to depositors, he added, such as lower, minimum requirements for checking accounts to avoid service charges. Before then, a checking account customer needed at least a $5,000 balance in his or her account to avoid a service charge or a total balance of $7,500 in all accounts at the bank. Now, this has been lowered to $3,000 and $5,000, respectively.
"We also reduced some of the business charges for checking accounts," Wilson said.

Another benefit involved the bank's issuance of a Mastercard-debit card that could be used at the bank's 1,640 ATMs or in making purchases at local stores. By using funds available in the customer's checking account, said Wilson, the card can be used as a replacement for cash or checks, minimising the use of either.
"We issued 700,000 of these cards and are doing over 160,000 transactions a week in various retail establishments," he said. "We think that this is a good deal for the bank and for our customers."
Why was the Chase name chosen instead of Chemical for the merged bank? "We felt that Chase had a more powerful name for the future," he said.

Chemical, founded in 1823, became the nation's third-largest bank when it merged with Manufacturers Hanover Corporation in 1991. But Chase, the sixth-largest U.S. bank, is older, having been founded in 1799. Chemical's name stems from its outgrowth from the New York Chemical Manufacturing Company, a dummy company launched to obtain a charter from the legislature, which would give them only to banks affiliated with a business.
Chase derives its name from Salmon P. Chase, secretary of the Treasury in Abraham Lincoln's cabinet.
In recent years, Chemical's advertising theme was, "Expect More from Us." Chase's was "Profit from the Experience."
Both are being scrapped in favour of the new blurb, "The Right Relationship Is Everything." What does it signify?
"It means that Chase is committed to giving our customers a sense of personal flexibility toward them," said Wilson.

With that pitch, the banking giant was telling its customers it could be just as responsive as any local bank, and making a veiled reference to the merger as the "right relationship," as well. Chase's smaller bank rivals, however, appear to be rallying either to end-run or sweep up the leavings of the big merger as it closes 100 branches.

"We think that the creation of this great giant is really an opportunity for community banks like us," said Gerald C. Keegan, chairman of the Greater New York Savings Bank, which operates 14 branches, including nine in Brooklyn. "We have built our business on our relationship with the people in the community. This merger will allow us to continue that by capitalising on the people displaced by the Chemical-Chase branch closings."
By community relationships, he added, Keegan said his bank believes Brooklyn's big population and diverse ethnic groups "hold expansion potential for us. We're equipped for it, too."
With ATM's that speak six languages and many multilingual employees, the bank tries to suit its diverse clientele, he said.
"In general, our experience is that people don't concern themselves with the size of the bank they deposit in," Keegan said. "They want security and service foremost."

Responding to Keegan, Chase's Wilson said, "He's definitely wrong when he talks about our displaced customers. The branches we are closing were duplications, often just across the street from one of our larger branches, so that depositors can now go there."

Bank mergers succeed based on the degree to which the banks' best customers feel wanted and attended to following the merger, said James McCormick, president of the First Manhattan Consulting Group, which advises Chase.

"The most sophisticated bank integrators are spending a disproportionate amount of time making sure that the best customers aren't being disrupted while trying to make their deal as seamless as possible," McCormick said.
